- ✓ **A. (correct):** Cloud Trace follows single requests across services and pinpoints the dependency that adds latency, which averages on service dashboards cannot show.
- ✗ **B. Uptime checks:** they probe availability from outside and say nothing about internal calls between microservices.
- ✗ **C. Cloud Profiler:** it attributes CPU and memory to code inside a service and does not give per-request timelines across services.
- ✗ **D. Error-count metrics:** slow requests often succeed and write no error entry, so a count of errors misses them.

## Key idea
Use Cloud Trace for per-request latency across services, Profiler for code-level resource use, and metrics and logs for aggregates and events.
Q009081:
## Continuous profiling in production
Cloud Profiler is a statistical, low-overhead profiler that continuously gathers CPU usage and memory-allocation information from production applications and attributes it to the source code that uses it. Test environments rarely reproduce production pressures, and microbenchmarks often fail to reflect real traffic. Profiler collects a profile of about 10 seconds every minute for one instance, with overhead during collection under 5 percent and commonly below 0.5 percent when amortized across replicas, which makes always-on profiling affordable. It supports languages such as Go, Java, Node.js and Python on Compute Engine, GKE, App Engine and other environments.
## Why this fits
The question is "which code consumes resources in production", not "which request is slow" (Trace) or "is the service up" (uptime checks).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One-time microbenchmark:** staging and synthetic load do not reproduce the production pattern, and the stated problem is that the lab does not show it.
- ✗ **B. Verbose debug logging:** it adds log volume and cost, may itself slow the service, and does not measure CPU by function.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Profiler attributes production CPU and heap usage to functions at very low overhead, so the team sees what the lab could not reproduce and can reduce compute need at the source.
- ✗ **D. More nodes:** this treats the symptom, raises cost and leaves the inefficient code in place.

## Key idea
Use Cloud Profiler for continuous, low-overhead production profiling that attributes CPU and memory to code.
Q009082:
## Alert on symptoms and budget burn, not on every cause
- A **retest window** (the condition's duration) keeps a condition from being met by a single measurement; set it long enough to cut false positives yet short enough to alert in good time.
- **Burn-rate alerts** on an SLO notify you when the error budget is consumed faster than a threshold. A burn rate above 1 means that, if sustained, the service will miss its SLO for the period. Google recommends two policies: a **fast-burn** alert (short lookback, a sudden large consumption, page immediately) and a **slow-burn** alert (longer lookback, steady erosion, a ticket or lower urgency).
- Page only for conditions that need human action now and reflect customer impact; route the rest to tickets or dashboards.
## Why the checkout outage was missed
CPU on individual VMs was fine while requests failed; a symptom-based SLO alert on checkout success would have fired within minutes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Everything to the pager:** indiscriminate paging produces alert fatigue and ignored alerts, as EHR-style incidents show.
- ✗ **B. No alerts in business hours:** customers become the monitoring system, and detection time grows.
- ✓ **C. Burn-rate alerts on a checkout SLO (correct):** they measure what the customer experiences, so a 20-minute error outage is caught, and the fast-burn and slow-burn pair separates urgent from gradual problems.
- ✗ **D. Lower thresholds and shorter windows:** this multiplies the noisy, low-value alerts while still ignoring checkout errors.
- ✓ **E. (correct):** Symptom paging with cause signals in dashboards and longer retest windows: this removes pages that need no action and avoids reacting to single spikes.

## Key idea
Page on customer-visible symptoms using SLO burn-rate alerts and retest windows; keep cause-level signals out of the pager.
Q009083:
## Measuring from the outside
Public uptime checks test the availability of publicly accessible URLs and Google Cloud resources by sending periodic HTTP, HTTPS or TCP requests from multiple locations around the world; an uptime check uses at least three checkers, and a check fails when no response arrives within the timeout from more than one location. You can attach an alerting policy and notification channels, ideally of more than one type. Private uptime checks exist for endpoints that are not public.
## Why internal signals miss this
Metrics and logs from the servers only describe requests that arrive. If DNS, a network path or a load balancer problem stops requests reaching the service, the servers look healthy. An external probe measures the customer's path and gives a direct availability measurement for SLO and SLA reporting.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Log-based metric:** requests that never arrive are never logged by the application, so the logs show nothing wrong.
- ✗ **B. Weekly manual test:** it is infrequent, from one location, and cannot support a 99.9% availability promise or timely alerts.
- ✗ **C. CPU alert:** an unreachable API receives no traffic, so CPU would drop rather than rise, and the alert would not fire.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A public uptime check from several locations tests what customers experience, including DNS and network paths, and its alerting policy notifies the team when the endpoint cannot be reached.

## Key idea
Use uptime checks for an external, customer-view availability measurement; internal metrics cannot see requests that never arrive.
Q009084:
## Dynamic routing mode
Cloud Router exchanges routes with on-premises (or other cloud) routers over BGP. What it advertises and which routes it installs is controlled by the **dynamic routing mode** of the VPC network.
- **Regional** (the default) dynamic routing: a Cloud Router advertises only the subnets in its own region and installs learned routes only for resources in its own region.
- **Global** dynamic routing: a Cloud Router advertises the subnets of all regions in the VPC network, and learned on-premises routes apply to all regions.
The mode is a property of the VPC network, not of one router or tunnel. A hybrid design that spans regions should decide on the mode deliberately, because it also determines which regions can use a learned route. Keep in mind that firewalls act only after a route exists: a missing route looks like a connectivity failure but no firewall change will fix it.
## Example
A VPC network with `us-central1` and `europe-west1` subnets and one Cloud Router in `us-central1`: with regional mode, on-premises learns only the `us-central1` ranges; with global mode it learns both.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More tunnels in us-central1:** extra tunnels add throughput and redundancy, not extra advertised prefixes. The prefixes announced depend on the routing mode.
- ✓ **B. Global dynamic routing (correct):** the symptom (only the router's own region is advertised) is exactly how regional mode behaves, and switching the VPC network to global mode makes the same Cloud Router advertise every region's subnets without new tunnels.
- ✗ **C. Static-route tunnels in europe-west1:** BGP is not limited to one region; the limit comes from the routing mode. A second set of tunnels with static routes adds cost and loses dynamic route exchange without fixing the cause.
- ✗ **D. Firewall rule:** firewall rules filter packets that already have a route. On-premises routers never learned the europe-west1 prefixes, so the traffic is not even sent into the tunnels.

## Key idea
When on-premises sees only one region's subnets, check the VPC network's dynamic routing mode: global lets one Cloud Router serve all regions.
Q009085:
## Detection versus prevention in the network
Google Cloud offers two intrusion services with different positions in the traffic path.
- **Cloud IDS** mirrors traffic with Packet Mirroring to Google-managed inspection VMs. It detects and alerts, but it does not take action to prevent an attack.
- **Cloud NGFW intrusion prevention service** (Cloud NGFW Enterprise) intercepts matching traffic and sends it to a Google-managed, zonal **firewall endpoint** that scans it against threat signatures. If a threat is found, the action set in the security profile (for example alert or deny) is applied to that packet.
## Building blocks
- A **firewall endpoint** per zone where workloads run, associated with the VPC network.
- A **security profile** of type `threat-prevention` collected in a **security profile group**.
- **Firewall policy rules** whose action references the security profile group, so only matching traffic is intercepted for Layer 7 inspection.
Because it is a firewall policy rule, it covers east-west traffic inside the network, unlike a control that only sits on an external load balancer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Cloud NGFW with endpoints, a threat-prevention profile group and policy rules: traffic that matches the rule is intercepted and inspected inline by a managed endpoint, and the profile action can drop it, which meets both the inline and the no-appliance requirement.
- ✗ **B. Cloud Armor:** it protects traffic that enters through supported load balancers and does not see VM-to-VM traffic inside the VPC network, so it cannot cover east-west inspection.
- ✗ **C. Manual deny lists:** IP-based rules cannot match exploit signatures or command-and-control behavior, and a weekly refresh is always behind, while attackers also use compromised internal hosts.
- ✗ **D. Cloud IDS:** it inspects mirrored copies out of band and only alerts. It helps detection, but it does not block anything, so it fails the prevention requirement.

## Key idea
Block threats inline in the VPC with Cloud NGFW Enterprise (firewall endpoints plus security profile groups); Cloud IDS only detects.
Q009086:
## Network tags versus secure tags
- **Network tags** are strings on a VM. Anyone who can edit the instance metadata can add or remove them, so a firewall rule keyed to a tag is only as strong as the edit permission on every VM.
- **Secure tags** are Resource Manager tags governed by IAM. Creating the tag and binding it to a resource need explicit permissions, so a security team can keep that power to itself. Cloud NGFW network firewall policies use secure tags as sources and targets.
Using identity-based match criteria means rules follow workloads when IP addresses change and cannot be changed by simply editing a VM.
## Why not just use ranges
IP ranges are a coarse control: any VM placed in the subnet gets the same access, and ranges must be updated when workloads move.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Separate zone:** firewall rules are VPC-wide and not scoped by zone, so zone placement does not limit who can reach the database.
- ✗ **B. Tag naming conventions:** documentation does not stop a developer with edit rights from adding a tag, so the control remains advisory.
- ✓ **C. Secure tags with restricted binding permission (correct):** the rule matches a workload attribute that only the security group can bind, which closes the gap that network tags leave open.
- ✗ **D. Subnet range rule:** it grants access to every VM in that range regardless of its role, and it is not a statement about who can alter a workload's identity. It also does not follow workloads that move.

## Key idea
Use IAM-governed secure tags in firewall policies when the rule must not be bypassable by anyone with VM edit rights.
Q009087:
## Passthrough versus proxy load balancers
- **Passthrough Network Load Balancers** do not terminate connections. Packets reach the backend VMs with the original client source IP, and the backend answers the client directly (direct server return). They handle TCP, UDP and other IP protocols, and external ones are regional.
- **Proxy load balancers** (Application Load Balancers and proxy Network Load Balancers) terminate the client connection and open a new one to the backend. The backend sees the proxy's address unless a header (for HTTP) or PROXY protocol carries the client address, and they are limited to the protocols they support.
## Selection logic
Start from the protocol and the requirements: UDP plus preserving client IP plus no termination points to a regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer. Choose a global Application Load Balancer for HTTP(S) needing global anycast, URL routing, Cloud CDN or Cloud Armor.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer:** it is only reachable from inside a VPC network or connected networks, so internet players could not use it.
- ✓ **B. Regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer (correct):** it forwards UDP packets without terminating them, the servers see the real source IP, and no proxy sits in the data path.
- ✗ **C. Global external Application Load Balancer:** it only carries HTTP(S)-family traffic, and it terminates the client connection, so UDP game traffic and original source addresses do not fit.
- ✗ **D. Global external proxy Network Load Balancer:** it proxies TCP and terminates the connection, which is not UDP and not a way to expose the source address natively.

## Key idea
UDP with preserved client IP and no termination: regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer; HTTP(S) needs an Application Load Balancer.
Q009088:
## Internal load balancing across regions
- A **regional internal Application Load Balancer** has backends in a single region. Enabling **global access** lets clients from other regions connect to it, but if that region fails the backends go with it.
- A **cross-region internal Application Load Balancer** is a multi-region, Envoy-based managed load balancer. Its backend service can hold backends in several regions, traffic goes to the backend closest to the client's forwarding rule, and if one region's backends are down, traffic fails over to another region.
- **Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers** are regional: backends and failover stay in one region, so a regional outage needs a manual switch to another load balancer's address.
## Fit to the EHR requirement
The case calls for at least 99.9% availability for customer-facing systems and had past outages from misconfiguration and spikes. Each region's VIP is allocated from a subnet in that region, so VIPs from several regions share the same global backend service and DNS routing policies steer clients to a responding VIP. Automatic cross-region failover removes a manual step in an incident.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Cross-region internal Application Load Balancer (correct):** one backend service with backends in both regions, automatic failover to healthy backends, VIPs from each region published under one DNS name with a DNS routing policy, and no internet exposure.
- ✗ **B. Per-region passthrough balancers:** each is regional with no cross-region failover, so clients must switch addresses by hand, which slows recovery and depends on a person during the incident.
- ✗ **C. Regional external ALB:** it has a public address, which violates the not reachable from the internet requirement; firewall filtering does not make the front end internal.
- ✗ **D. Regional internal ALB with global access:** global access only changes who can connect. All backends sit in one region, so a regional outage still takes the API down.

## Key idea
Internal service that must survive a regional failure without manual switching: cross-region internal Application Load Balancer.
Q009089:
## Auto mode versus custom mode
- **Auto mode** VPC networks automatically create one subnet in every region from a predefined block, and add subnets for new regions. The default network is auto mode.
- **Custom mode** VPC networks start with no subnets; you create subnets in chosen regions with ranges you specify.
Auto mode is convenient for experiments. For production the ranges matter: Cloud VPN, Interconnect and VPC Network Peering all need non-overlapping subnet ranges between connected networks, and auto mode's predefined block can collide with on-premises or other VPC networks. An auto mode network can be converted to custom mode, but never back.
## Common misconceptions
Hybrid connectivity, Private Google Access and firewall behavior are available in both modes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cloud Router claim:** Cloud Router and its BGP sessions work with auto mode networks as well; the mode is not a hybrid prerequisite.
- ✗ **B. Implied rules claim:** the implied deny-ingress rule exists in both modes. Access between peered networks is granted by firewall rules, not by the network mode.
- ✗ **C. Private Google Access claim:** Private Google Access is a per-subnet setting available in both modes.
- ✓ **D. Choose ranges (correct):** custom mode lets you plan non-overlapping addressing across on-premises, peering and other VPC networks, which hybrid and peering designs require.
- ✓ **E. Chosen regions only (correct):** you create subnets only where workloads run, which keeps address space tidy and limits where resources can be placed.

## Key idea
Production, hybrid and peered networks need planned, non-overlapping ranges, so use custom mode VPC networks.
Q009090:
## Multicloud connectivity options
- **HA VPN** is quick to build and encrypted but crosses the public internet, with per-tunnel bandwidth limits and variable latency.
- **Cross-Cloud Interconnect** is a dedicated physical connection between the Google network and the network of a supported cloud provider. Google provisions and supports the connection up to the point where it reaches the other provider's network, so the customer does not install equipment in a colocation facility. The VPC network is peered with the network hosted by the other provider.
- **Dedicated Interconnect** or **Partner Interconnect** can also reach another cloud, but the customer then orders and operates the routing and cross-connects at a facility or provider.
## Caveat
Google does not guarantee the other provider's uptime, so a support case must also be opened with that provider.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. HA VPN:** traffic crosses the internet and per-tunnel throughput is limited, which does not suit tens of gigabits of sustained private exchange.
- ✗ **B. Partner Interconnect:** it relies on carrier circuits the team arranges, adding operational work that the requirement for a Google-provisioned link is meant to avoid.
- ✓ **C. Cross-Cloud Interconnect (correct):** Google-provisioned dedicated capacity to the other cloud, private traffic, and no customer-owned equipment at a colocation facility.
- ✗ **D. Direct Peering:** it exchanges traffic with Google's public edge for Google services and is not a private path between the VPC network and another cloud.

## Key idea
Private, high-bandwidth VPC-to-other-cloud links without your own colocation gear point to Cross-Cloud Interconnect.
Q009091:
## Controlled outbound internet access
Private VMs and nodes need a way to reach the internet without exposing inbound access.
- **Cloud NAT** (public NAT) translates outbound traffic to IP addresses held by the NAT gateway. It is software-defined: no proxy VMs, and it works on a gateway attached to a Cloud Router in one region for chosen subnet ranges.
- With **automatic** address allocation, Cloud NAT adds addresses as needed, so the set can change. With **manual** allocation you reserve static external addresses, which gives suppliers a stable set to allowlist.
- For GKE private clusters, include the Pod secondary range if Pods must reach the internet.
## What does not help
**Private Google Access** only reaches Google APIs and services, not third-party endpoints, and route advertisements affect routing, not the source address seen by suppliers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom advertisements:** they influence which prefixes a Cloud Router announces to peers and do not change the source address of outbound internet traffic.
- ✓ **B. Cloud NAT with reserved static addresses (correct):** outbound supplier calls come from a small stable address set, nodes stay private, and scaling does not change what suppliers see.
- ✗ **C. Private Google Access:** it provides access to Google APIs without external IPs, not to supplier endpoints on the internet.
- ✗ **D. Ephemeral node IPs:** addresses change with node replacement and autoscaling, the nodes would become directly internet-addressable, and the allowlist would need constant edits.

## Key idea
Fixed, allowlistable egress for private workloads means Cloud NAT with manually allocated static IP addresses.
Q009092:
## Hybrid DNS in Cloud DNS
Name resolution must work in both directions, and both directions are configured with Cloud DNS features on the VPC network.
- **Inbound server policy**: creates inbound entry points, which are internal IP addresses in the VPC network. On-premises resolvers forward queries for the cloud zone to those addresses, so on-premises systems can resolve private Cloud DNS records.
- **Forwarding zone** (outbound forwarding): Cloud DNS forwards queries for a given domain to target name servers, such as the on-premises DNS servers, so VMs resolve on-premises names with no per-VM changes.
Routes and firewall rules must allow the DNS traffic between the networks across the hybrid link.
## Why a public zone is wrong
Internal names should not be published publicly, and public resolution would not reach private addresses.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hosts files:** the record sets drift out of date, and this does not scale or support dynamic names.
- ✗ **B. Secondary zone and manual VM settings:** pointing VMs at on-premises servers manually creates per-VM configuration and bypasses Cloud DNS, so the private zone is no longer resolved from the VMs.
- ✗ **C. Public zone:** it would publish internal names and addresses on the internet, and the private records in the Cloud DNS private zone would not be used.
- ✓ **D. Inbound server policy plus a forwarding zone (correct):** each side forwards the other's domain to the right resolver over the private link, with no changes on individual VMs.

## Key idea
Use an inbound server policy for on-premises-to-cloud and a forwarding zone for cloud-to-on-premises resolution.
Q009093:
## Steering traffic between hybrid paths
Cloud Router learns routes over BGP and installs them in the VPC network. When multiple paths exist for the same prefix, route priority decides which is used.
- Cloud Router sessions have a **base route priority** (the MED sent for advertised routes); for learned routes it is the priority of the installed dynamic route. **Lower values are preferred.**
- Equal priorities on equal-prefix routes allow ECMP-style distribution across paths.
## Design rule
For an active/standby design, give the primary path the lower number and the backup the higher number. The VPN then takes traffic only when the Interconnect routes are withdrawn. Never remove the backup: it protects from the failure of the primary, and Google's redundancy guidance for critical workloads keeps independent paths.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Lower priority value on the Interconnect (correct):** the Interconnect routes win while they exist, and the VPN routes become active only when they fail, which gives low-latency primary and resilient standby.
- ✗ **B. Higher number on the Interconnect:** lower values win, so this would prefer the VPN, which makes the latency problem worse.
- ✗ **C. Equal priority:** this lets the VPN carry a share of the traffic, which is the symptom the team is complaining about.
- ✗ **D. Deleting the VPN:** removing the backup reduces resilience, so one fault in the Interconnect topology could cut off the plant.

## Key idea
In Cloud Router, the lower priority value (MED) wins; give the primary path the lower value and keep the backup at a higher value.
Q009094:
## Hybrid load balancing
Cloud Load Balancing treats on-premises and other-cloud services like any other backend, but it needs an endpoint definition that points outside Google Cloud.
- A **hybrid connectivity NEG** holds endpoints as valid `IP:port` combinations that the load balancer can reach over Cloud VPN, Cloud Interconnect or router appliance VMs. It works with global external Application Load Balancers among others.
- An **internet NEG** instead references a public FQDN or IP and sends traffic over the internet.
- A **serverless NEG** points to Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions or App Engine.
## Why it fits modernization
A URL map can route `/ingest` to the hybrid NEG while other paths go to GKE backends, so users see one hostname while services move over time. Health checks must be able to reach the on-premises endpoints, so the firewall there must allow Google's health check probes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Internet NEG:** it sends requests across the public internet to a public name, which ignores the requirement to use the Interconnect.
- ✗ **B. Serverless NEG:** it targets Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions or App Engine services, not arbitrary on-premises servers.
- ✗ **C. Managed instance group:** instance groups contain Compute Engine VMs, so on-premises servers cannot be members.
- ✓ **D. Hybrid connectivity NEG (correct):** private on-premises IP:port endpoints become a normal backend, the URL map splits paths between GKE and the data center, and traffic stays on the Interconnect.

## Key idea
To put on-premises backends behind a Google Cloud load balancer over Interconnect or VPN, use a hybrid connectivity NEG.
Q009095:
## How Cloud IDS works
Cloud IDS creates a Google-managed peered network with inspection VMs. A zonal **IDS endpoint** receives mirrored traffic (from any zone in its region), and **Packet Mirroring policies** attached to it choose which VMs, subnets or tags are copied, optionally filtered by protocol, address range or direction. Inspection uses Palo Alto Networks threat technologies.
- Because it works on copies, it is out of band: no latency or failure risk for production traffic.
- It sees north-south and east-west traffic, including intra-subnet traffic that routing controls never touch.
- It detects and alerts but takes no action. Prevention is done with a control such as Cloud NGFW.
## Scale
Plan an endpoint per region to monitor, and more than one where throughput is high, since each has a finite inspection capacity.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Inline dropping by Cloud IDS:** it inspects mirrored copies, so it cannot drop live packets.
- ✗ **B. One endpoint for all regions:** an endpoint inspects traffic from zones in its own region, and you create endpoints for each region you want to monitor.
- ✓ **C. Follow-up with Cloud NGFW (correct):** Cloud IDS only alerts, so blocking or other action comes from a separate control such as Cloud NGFW policies.
- ✗ **D. Cloud Armor:** it protects traffic at supported load balancers and does not see VM-to-VM traffic inside subnets.
- ✓ **E. Endpoint with mirroring policies (correct):** mirroring copies the chosen traffic, including intra-subnet flows, to a regional endpoint for inspection without being inline.

## Key idea
Cloud IDS is out-of-band detection through packet mirroring in each monitored region; pair it with Cloud NGFW to act on findings.
Q009096:
## Connecting serverless to a VPC network
Cloud Run can send outbound traffic to resources with internal IP addresses (Compute Engine VMs, Memorystore, on-premises through hybrid connectivity) in two ways.
- **Direct VPC egress** (recommended): the service's instances get addresses from a subnet of your VPC network and send traffic directly. There are no connector instances to manage.
- **Serverless VPC Access connectors**: a managed set of connector instances sits in between; they must be sized and add a component to run.
## Design points
- Plan subnet size, since Direct VPC egress consumes subnet addresses for running instances.
- Inbound traffic from a VPC network to Cloud Run does not go through either mechanism; it uses a load balancer or Private Service Connect.
- Firewall rules and Cloud NAT apply as for other resources on that subnet.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Direct VPC egress (correct):** instances connect straight into the subnet, so private Memorystore and on-premises destinations are reachable with no connector fleet to size.
- ✗ **B. Connector sizing:** connectors work, but they add instances to run and capacity to plan, which the team wants to avoid; docs recommend the direct approach.
- ✗ **C. Moving to GKE:** Cloud Run reaches private addresses through VPC connectivity, so a platform change is unnecessary.
- ✗ **D. Public Memorystore:** Memorystore is reached through private addressing, and an allowlist of dynamic serverless egress addresses does not provide a stable, secure design.

## Key idea
Cloud Run reaching private IP resources: prefer Direct VPC egress over Serverless VPC Access connectors, and size the subnet.
Q009097:
## Controlling how Cloud Run is reached
Cloud Run has an **ingress** setting that decides which sources can send requests to the service.
- **All**: any request, including the internet directly to the `run.app` URL.
- **Internal**: only requests from the VPC network and certain Google Cloud sources.
- **Internal and Cloud Load Balancing**: internal sources plus requests through an external Application Load Balancer, so internet traffic is subject to load balancer features such as Cloud Armor, Identity-Aware Proxy and Cloud CDN.
A **serverless NEG** makes the Cloud Run service a backend of the load balancer.
## Why it matters
If ingress stays on "all", users can skip the front door and every control attached to it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. VPC firewall rule:** Cloud Run's request path is not controlled by VPC firewall rules on the client's internet source, and the run.app endpoint is a Google-managed front end.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Ingress limited to internal and load balancing plus a serverless NEG: the load balancer path stays working while direct run.app requests from the internet are refused, so Cloud Armor cannot be bypassed.
- ✗ **C. Dropping the load balancer:** this removes Cloud Armor, custom domain and CDN features, the reverse of the goal.
- ✗ **D. Cloud NAT:** it translates outbound traffic from private resources and plays no role in inbound requests to Cloud Run.

## Key idea
Restrict Cloud Run ingress to internal and Cloud Load Balancing so the load balancer and its protections become the only internet entry point.
Q009098:
## Designing for preemption
Spot VMs use excess Compute Engine capacity at a deep discount, and Compute Engine can preempt them at any time. On preemption it either **stops** (default) or **deletes** the VM, depending on the termination action.
- Spot VMs cannot live migrate and cannot be set to restart automatically on host events, and they have no guaranteed availability.
- Spot VMs have no minimum or maximum runtime unless you limit it.
- Good fits are fault-tolerant, stateless or checkpointable batch work.
## Patterns
- Put workers in a **managed instance group** so lost capacity is replaced when resources return.
- Checkpoint to durable storage and handle the short shutdown window with a **shutdown script**.
- Keep components whose loss stops everything (queue, coordinator, state) on standard VMs or managed services.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. MIG with Spot template (correct):** the group replaces preempted workers when capacity is available, so the job continues without manual restarts.
- ✗ **B. Coordinator on Spot:** a preempted queue or coordinator stops the whole job, so these components should be on standard capacity.
- ✗ **C. Restart and live migration:** Spot VMs cannot be live migrated or auto-restarted on host events, so the job must handle interruptions itself.
- ✗ **D. 24-hour limit:** Spot VMs have no fixed maximum runtime and can be preempted at any time, so a 24-hour cap offers no protection.
- ✓ **E. Checkpoints and shutdown handling (correct):** progress survives preemption, so a repeated task does not restart from zero.

## Key idea
Spot VMs suit fault-tolerant work: use a MIG to replace capacity, checkpoint progress, and keep critical coordinators on standard VMs.
Q009099:
## VMware workloads on Google Cloud
**Google Cloud VMware Engine** runs the VMware stack (vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX, HCX) on Google Cloud bare metal infrastructure. Tools, skills and processes carry over, and the environment integrates with Google Cloud services.
- **HCX** is deployed automatically with the private cloud and supports bulk and vMotion migrations and extending Layer 2 networks, so VMs can keep their IP addresses and be moved in waves. (VMware Engine also documents NSX Layer 2 VPN stretching, after which no new IP assignment is required.)
- It requires private connectivity (Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect) between the sites.
## Trade-offs
Converting to Compute Engine or containers gives deeper cloud-native benefits and potentially lower cost over time, but takes more change work (re-addressing, new tooling, application changes). With a closing data center and hard-coded addresses, VMware Engine buys time, and modernization can follow later.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Convert and re-address:** it changes IP addresses that plant systems depend on, forcing changes in every connected system before the deadline.
- ✓ **B. VMware Engine with HCX (correct):** the VMware platform and skills stay the same, networks can be extended so addresses stay unchanged, and waves limit downtime, which meets the deadline.
- ✗ **C. Rewrite first:** a full containerization before moving takes longer than the data center closure allows and carries high risk.
- ✗ **D. Nightly exports:** file copies do not provide a controlled cutover, keep running state or maintain addresses, and restoring them all on closing day is a risky big-bang.

## Key idea
For fast, low-change VMware moves that preserve addresses and skills, use VMware Engine with HCX, then modernize later.
Q009100:
## Infrastructure as code on Google Cloud
Deployment Manager reached end of support on 2026-03-31, so new work uses **Terraform**, the declarative standard, or **Infrastructure Manager**, a managed service that deploys Terraform configurations stored in Cloud Storage, Git repositories or local directories and tracks deployments and revisions.
- The same module, parameterized with variables, produces consistent dev, staging, production and per-customer environments.
- Pull request review on the Git repository gives the change control that the case's outages (misconfiguration) call for.
- Deployments and revisions provide the lifecycle and history of what was applied.
## Imperative versus declarative
Scripts and manual steps describe how to do each step and drift between environments. Declarative IaC describes the desired state and can be re-applied.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Deployment Manager:** support ended on 2026-03-31, so building new environments on it adds risk and no future fixes.
- ✗ **B. gcloud scripts:** imperative steps edited by hand differ between runs, are hard to review and do not track state, which invites the misconfigurations in the case.
- ✓ **C. Terraform in Git deployed through Infrastructure Manager (correct):** consistent parameterized environments, peer-reviewed changes and tracked revisions, on a supported toolchain.
- ✗ **D. Console runbook:** manual steps are slow, error-prone and not repeatable, and screenshots are not an enforceable record.

## Key idea
Repeatable environments with reviewed change: Terraform in Git with Infrastructure Manager (not Deployment Manager).
Q009101:
## Patch management on Compute Engine
**VM Manager** includes **OS patch management** with two parts.
- **Patch deployment**: automates applying OS and software patches. A deployment schedules **patch jobs** that run across selected VMs (by zone, name or label) with options such as rolling out zone by zone and setting a disruption budget.
- **Patch compliance**: shows patch status across Windows and Linux VMs and gives recommendations.
It requires the OS Config API and the OS Config agent on VMs; the agent uses each OS's update mechanism and package sources. If VMs have no external IP, external update sources can be reached through Cloud NAT or a proxy.
## Why centralized beats per-VM scripts
A central schedule, rollout limits and compliance data provide governance across hundreds of VMs, which per-VM jobs cannot give.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Vendor defaults:** updates occur at uncoordinated times, so many VMs may restart together, and nobody can report which are patched.
- ✗ **B. SSH from Cloud Build:** it needs credentials and network access to all VMs, offers no rollout limits and no patch inventory, and is fragile.
- ✗ **C. Cron scripts:** no central control over rollout pace, no consistent result across Windows and Linux, and no compliance reporting.
- ✓ **D. VM Manager patch deployments (correct):** recurring schedules for both operating systems, controlled rollout by zone and a disruption budget, plus compliance reports in one place.

## Key idea
Patch fleets with VM Manager: scheduled patch deployments, controlled rollout and compliance reporting.
Q009102:
## Immutable infrastructure with MIGs
A MIG creates identical VMs from an **instance template**. Instead of changing running VMs (mutable), build a new image or template and let the MIG replace instances.
- A **rolling update** gradually replaces instances with ones from the new template. The **maximum surge** adds extra instances temporarily and **maximum unavailable** limits capacity lost, so the service keeps serving.
- Health checks and autohealing validate new instances, and you can roll back by pointing to the previous template.
- Every VM starts from the same tested image, so no drift.
## Where in-place patching still fits
Long-lived pet VMs and stateful servers use patch management tools; for stateless tiers replacement is more reliable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lower autoscaler target:** autoscaling adds or removes instances by load and doesn't ensure that older instances are replaced; the new image would not be applied systematically.
- ✓ **B. New patched template and a rolling update (correct):** replacements come from one tested image, capacity is protected by surge and unavailable limits, and a rollback is simple.
- ✗ **C. Bulk weekend patching:** it keeps the in-place drift and risk, and patching all instances at once removes the capacity safeguards.
- ✗ **D. Recreating the group:** deleting the group causes an outage that a rolling update avoids.

## Key idea
For stateless tiers, patch by replacing instances from a new template with a controlled rolling update.
Q009103:
## Controlling GKE maintenance
GKE upgrades control planes and nodes automatically for clusters enrolled in a **release channel**, which delivers tested versions at a defined pace.
- A **maintenance window** limits when automated maintenance such as auto-upgrades can start, for example weekday evenings.
- A **maintenance exclusion** blocks defined kinds of maintenance during a period, for example a key sales event.
- Together they keep the automation while protecting critical business periods.
## Risks of opting out
Turning off automation increases toil and the chance of running unsupported or unpatched versions. Replacing clusters for each event is a heavy approach for a problem that scheduling already solves.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Release channel, a maintenance window and an exclusion for the sales event: upgrades remain automatic outside protected times, and nothing disruptive happens during the event.
- ✗ **B. Static version with no channel:** the cluster is not kept current, loses the release channel's tested cadence, and reaches end of support without a plan.
- ✗ **C. Permanent manual upgrades:** this depends on memory, so clusters fall behind on security patches and unsupported versions become likely.
- ✗ **D. A second cluster for the event:** building and removing a cluster is high effort and risk compared with using the built-in exclusion.

## Key idea
Combine a release channel with maintenance windows and exclusions to keep GKE current while avoiding critical business periods.
Q009104:
## Private GKE clusters
In a **private cluster**, nodes have only internal IP addresses. Two separate paths need design.
- **Control plane access**: engineers use the endpoint, which you can restrict with **authorized networks** so only listed CIDR ranges can connect.
- **Outbound access from nodes and Pods** to the internet (public registries, SaaS APIs): use **Cloud NAT**, since private nodes have no external IPs. Include the Pod ranges in the NAT configuration where Pods originate traffic.
- **Private Google Access** only gives private nodes access to Google APIs and services, not arbitrary internet sites.
## Security rationale
Giving nodes external IPs undoes the isolation that private nodes provide.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disabling firewalling:** there is no such control, and removing protection widens exposure instead of limiting access to corporate ranges.
- ✗ **B. External IPs on nodes:** nodes become directly addressable from the internet, which defeats the purpose of a private cluster.
- ✓ **C. Cloud NAT (correct):** private nodes and Pods get controlled outbound-only internet access for the registry and the SaaS API without any inbound exposure.
- ✗ **D. Private Google Access:** it covers Google APIs only, so third-party registries and SaaS endpoints still cannot be reached.
- ✓ **E. Authorized networks (correct):** only the corporate ranges can reach the control plane endpoint, which matches the access requirement.

## Key idea
Private GKE: restrict the control plane with authorized networks and give private nodes outbound access through Cloud NAT.
Q009105:
## Autoscaling for slow-starting applications
A MIG autoscaler normally reacts to real-time metrics. If an application needs minutes to initialize, instances added after load rises arrive too late.
- **Predictive autoscaling** forecasts load from its history of daily and weekly cycles and adds instances ahead of the predicted increase, so capacity is ready when the rise arrives. It suits long initialization times and predictable cycles.
- The **initialization period** tells the autoscaler how long a new instance takes to start serving, so it does not use that instance's metrics prematurely.
- **Scheduled** autoscaling uses fixed capacity values at chosen times, good for known events but not for peaks that change size.
## Trade-off
Predictive scaling combines with reactive scaling, which still handles unexpected spikes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Zonal group:** this lowers resilience and does not shorten application initialization, which is the cause of the delay.
- ✗ **B. Fixed schedule:** one fixed minimum either wastes money on small days or under-provisions on large ones, and does not follow the varying peaks.
- ✗ **C. Delayed scale-out:** it slows additions of instances and increases the lag the team is trying to remove.
- ✓ **D. Predictive autoscaling plus a matching initialization period (correct):** capacity is added before the learned morning rise, and variable peak sizes are still followed by the reactive part.

## Key idea
For slow-starting apps with repeating load patterns, use predictive autoscaling with a correct initialization period.
Q009106:
## Dedicated hosts for licensing and isolation
A **sole-tenant node** is a physical Compute Engine server dedicated to one project's VMs. Nodes are grouped in **node groups**, and **node affinity labels** on VMs control which nodes they use.
- Sole-tenant nodes support bring your own license (BYOL) cases that need per-core or per-processor licenses. Compute Engine reports the ID of the physical server a VM runs on, so usage can be reviewed in Cloud Logging.
- A **host maintenance policy** controls how VMs behave when their host is updated, including whether they keep affinity with a specific server.
- They also meet requirements for physical isolation from other customers.
## Why other settings do not help
Machine size, discounts and encryption features change cost or security, not which physical cores a license counts or how to evidence them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Sole-tenant nodes with node affinity (correct):** VMs stay on dedicated hosts, the number of cores and servers is known, and logged server IDs give evidence for the audit.
- ✗ **B. Shielded VMs and Confidential Computing:** they protect integrity and data in use, but give no per-host core accounting for a license.
- ✗ **C. Spot with committed use:** these are pricing and provisioning models and do not control hosts; Spot VMs can also be preempted.
- ✗ **D. Larger standard VM:** it runs on shared hosts, so physical core counts and server identity cannot be demonstrated.

## Key idea
Per-core licensing and physical-host audit evidence point to sole-tenant nodes with node affinity.
Q009107:
## Spot VMs in GKE
GKE node pools can use Spot VMs, which behave like standard GKE nodes but with no guarantee of availability. When Compute Engine reclaims the capacity, GKE receives a preemption notice, and Pods have a short graceful termination period (30 seconds by default, shared with critical system Pods; it can be extended to 120 seconds).
- Use Spot node pools for fault-tolerant, stateless or restartable workloads.
- Keep critical components on standard nodes.
- Use a **taint** on the Spot pool with a matching **toleration** and **node selector** in workloads, so only intended Pods land there. Autopilot can handle this for Spot Pods automatically.
## Design for mixed workloads
Separate pools let one cluster serve both cost and reliability goals, with autoscaling per pool.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. All Spot:** preemptions can remove many nodes at once, including those running databases and system components, causing availability loss.
- ✗ **B. No Spot in the cluster:** it gives up the savings that fault-tolerant workloads can safely take.
- ✗ **C. Databases on Spot:** the graceful termination period is short (30 seconds by default, extendable only to 120), which is not a long warning and not enough for reliable stateful shutdown and recovery.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A separate Spot node pool for tolerant Pods, standard nodes for the rest: batch and stateless services get the discount, while databases and system components keep reliable capacity.

## Key idea
Mix GKE node pools: Spot for fault-tolerant Pods selected by taints and tolerations, standard for stateful and critical components.
Q009108:
## What a BAA does and does not do
In the United States, HIPAA applies to covered entities and their business associates. When a cloud provider handles protected health information (PHI) for you, a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is the contract that sets out its obligations. Google's HIPAA guidance says the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services offers no certification program for HIPAA, that compliance is a shared responsibility, and that the Google Cloud BAA covers the whole Google Cloud infrastructure (all regions) but only a listed set of products.
## Staying inside the covered products
- The guidance tells customers to disable unsupported services for PHI, and not to use pre-GA offerings with PHI unless the terms say so.
- The preventive control is an organization policy: the `gcp.restrictServiceUsage` constraint limits which service APIs a folder or project may use, so a mistake cannot happen by accident.
- Assured Workloads has a US Data Boundary for Healthcare and Life Sciences control package (in-scope services are on Google's HIPAA and HITRUST lists) that adds data boundary controls; it is an extra guardrail, not a legal prerequisite for HIPAA.
This is an architecture pattern, not legal advice; the compliance team still evaluates the obligations.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Single region:** the Google Cloud BAA covers the entire infrastructure, all regions and zones. Tying PHI to one region is a separate residency choice, not a condition of the BAA.
- ✗ **B. Regulator certificate:** HHS does not certify HIPAA compliance, so no such certificate exists for a project. Compliance is shown through your own controls and the shared responsibility model.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Accepting the BAA and then restricting allowed services at the folder level with an organization policy turns the "covered products only" rule into an enforced guardrail, and excluding pre-GA features follows the HIPAA guidance.
- ✗ **D. BAA blocks services:** a BAA is a contract, not a technical control. It does not stop anyone from enabling a service, so without a policy an engineer can send PHI to an uncovered product.

## Key idea
A BAA is a contract; enforce "covered services only" with organization policy and keep pre-GA features away from PHI.
Q009109:
## Where log retention can be set
Cloud Logging stores logs in log buckets. Every project has a `_Required` bucket (Admin Activity and System Event audit logs, fixed 400-day retention that cannot be changed) and a `_Default` bucket (default 30 days, configurable). Retention is configurable per user-defined bucket, between 1 and 3650 days.
## Centralizing and protecting it
- The docs state that you cannot extend the retention period of a log bucket that lives in a folder or organization. The supported pattern is a log sink routing those entries to a bucket in a project, then setting that bucket's retention.
- An aggregated sink at the organization or a folder routes logs from all child projects to one destination, giving one retention rule for all of them.
- Locking a bucket locks its retention policy: it can no longer be shortened, and the bucket cannot be deleted until every entry has met retention. Add a lien on the project to prevent accidental project deletion.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Required bucket:** the retention of the `_Required` bucket is fixed at 400 days and cannot be changed, so it can never be stretched to seven years.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** An aggregated sink to a dedicated project's log bucket gives one consistent retention setting for all projects, and locking the bucket stops anyone, including administrators of source projects, from reducing the period.
- ✗ **C. Per-project owners:** leaving the choice to each team is the opposite of consistent retention, and project-level administrators could also shorten it later. Nothing enforces seven years.
- ✗ **D. Extend org-level buckets:** the docs say the retention of a bucket in a folder or organization cannot be extended; the retention must be set on a bucket in a project that the sink targets.

## Key idea
Central, consistent retention: aggregated sink to a log bucket in a project, set retention there, then lock it.
Q009110:
## Certifications and shared responsibility
Google Cloud's compliance resource center lists independent certifications, attestations and audit reports (for example SOC 1, SOC 2, SOC 3, ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS) and offers the reports through the Compliance Reports Manager. These cover the controls that Google operates.
Compliance for a customer service is shared. The provider's reports cover facilities, infrastructure and the services it runs; the customer is responsible for how it configures and uses them: identities and access, data classification, network and application settings, logging and change processes. Auditors therefore expect evidence of both: the provider's report and the customer's own controls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automatic compliance:** a provider's attestation covers its own controls only. Services built on it must be shown to meet the criteria on their own.
- ✗ **B. All controls to Google:** the shared responsibility model leaves configuration and application-level controls with the customer, which is why they are in the audit scope.
- ✗ **C. Replaces audit logs:** Google does not keep a customer's activity records for the customer's audit. The customer configures, routes and retains its own logs, such as Cloud Audit Logs.
- ✓ **D. Provider reports (correct):** the Compliance Reports Manager gives the auditor Google's independent SOC 2 and other reports, which evidence the controls that the provider operates.
- ✓ **E. Customer controls (correct):** the customer still needs its own documented and operating controls for what it manages (access, change, monitoring), and the auditor tests those.

## Key idea
Provider reports prove the provider's controls; the customer must still show its own controls for what it configures and runs.
Q009111:
## Reducing the scope of cardholder data
PCI DSS applies to all systems, networks and applications that store, process or transmit cardholder data, plus systems that secure and log access to them. The less cardholder data spreads, the smaller that scope. Google Cloud's PCI-compliant services give a base to build on, but the customer remains responsible for its application's compliance.
## Removing the data early
Sensitive Data Protection can inspect text for infoTypes such as credit card numbers and de-identify them. Its transformations include redaction (delete the value), replacement, masking, crypto-based tokenization, bucketing and date shifting. For card numbers in transcripts, redaction or masking before storage means the analytics layer never holds the primary account number, so those systems stay out of the card environment.
The same idea applies to the original recordings: keep audio containing spoken card data in a tightly controlled location, or avoid capturing it at all.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Encrypt and keep the text:** encryption at rest protects the stored files but the data is still decrypted for every query and summary, so the downstream services still process cardholder data.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Detecting and redacting card numbers with Sensitive Data Protection before storage removes the data from analytics and gen AI summaries, which keeps those systems out of the cardholder data scope.
- ✗ **C. Delete transcripts later:** leaving the raw recordings with card data in the bucket indefinitely keeps cardholder data in scope, and the data still flowed through the analytics job.
- ✗ **D. Dataset permissions only:** access control limits who can read, but the card numbers still sit in every analytics table, so all those systems remain in PCI scope and any over-broad grant exposes them.

## Key idea
Reduce PCI scope by removing card data early: detect and redact it with Sensitive Data Protection before it reaches analytics.
Q009112:
## Provider certification is the base, not the answer
Google Cloud states that its products are reviewed by a Qualified Security Assessor against PCI DSS and that customers are still responsible for ensuring that their applications comply. A shared responsibility matrix explains which requirements Google covers and which remain with the customer.
## Narrowing scope
- Put the systems that handle cardholder data in their own project (or folders) and VPC, with firewall rules that allow only needed flows, so the rest of the estate stays outside the assessment.
- Log and monitor access to that environment, because systems that secure and log access to the card environment are in scope too.
- Use tokenization or a hosted payment page so card numbers reach as few systems as possible.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Google's assessed services form a compliant base, but the application, access and network settings are the retailer's responsibility; isolating the checkout in its own project and network reduces what must be assessed.
- ✗ **B. Managed services remove duties:** even with managed services the customer is responsible for access, configuration, data handling and its application code, so duties remain.
- ✗ **C. Impossible on shared infrastructure:** Google Cloud publishes a shared responsibility matrix and guidance for building PCI DSS environments there, so it is supported.
- ✗ **D. Inherited validation:** the provider's report evidences the provider's controls only. The retailer's own application still has to be assessed and shown to meet the requirements.

## Key idea
Certified services are a base; the customer's application and configuration still need assessment, and isolation shrinks that scope.
Q009113:
## What the architect designs for
COPPA is a U.S. regulation on collecting personal information online from children under 13 for services directed to them or with actual knowledge. Google's COPPA page describes how Workspace for Education can be used in compliance when a school provides parental consent; it does not make any customer application compliant. The architect therefore designs the data handling and leaves legal interpretation to counsel.
## Design patterns that help
- Data minimization: do not collect fields the product does not need.
- Isolation: a dedicated project or dataset for child data, with narrow IAM, so access can be reviewed and logged.
- Retention limits: table or partition expiration and Cloud Storage lifecycle rules so data does not live forever.
- Findability and deletion: an index (for example a user key) so records of one child can be located and removed, including from derived tables.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mix with adult data:** commingling makes it harder to apply stricter access, retention and deletion to child records, so rows would be harder, not easier, to find and remove.
- ✗ **B. Compliance page as proof:** the page does not certify customer applications. It explains Workspace for Education use, and customers remain responsible for their own collection practices.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Minimizing collection, isolating child data with narrow access, expiring it and being able to locate and delete one child's records are design controls that support the privacy obligations; legal confirmation is still the company's job.
- ✗ **D. Collect everything:** broad collection is the opposite of data minimization, and it creates more child data to protect, review and delete.

## Key idea
Support children's privacy by minimizing, isolating, expiring and being able to delete child data; the platform does not make the app compliant.
Q009114:
## Residency versus sovereignty controls
- **Data residency** means where the data is stored. The organization policy "resource locations" constraint (`gcp.resourceLocations`, with value groups such as `in:eu-locations`) restricts the locations in which supported resources can be created.
- **Personnel and support controls** are about who at the provider can access data when providing support. They are not part of a location constraint.
## What Assured Workloads adds
Assured Workloads applies a control package to a folder. The EU Data Boundary control package sets data location controls for EU-only regions; the "EU Data Boundary and Support" package also sets support access controls to EU-based personnel (a Premium tier); "with Access Justifications" adds key access justifications. The controls are enforced with organization policy constraints and other features, and Assured Workloads monitors for violations.
Always check the supported-products list of the package, because unsupported products have not met all its controls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cannot cover storage:** the constraint does cover supported storage services, such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery. A VPN protects traffic in transit and says nothing about where stored data lives.
- ✗ **B. Constraint covers personnel:** it does not. It only controls resource locations, so the support-personnel requirement would remain unmet.
- ✗ **C. Multi-region only:** the constraint accepts regions, multi-regions and value groups. Data Access audit logs record access but do not control it or where support staff are located.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A location constraint restricts where resources can be created, while personnel access is a separate requirement; an Assured Workloads folder with an EU package that includes support controls covers both.

## Key idea
Location policy gives residency; for EU-based support personnel too, use an Assured Workloads EU package with support controls.
Q009115:
## Location granularity matters
A BigQuery dataset has a location: either a region (for example `europe-west3`, Frankfurt) or a multi-region (`EU`, `US`). The EU multi-region stores data in EU locations but does not guarantee a particular country, so it does not satisfy a "stay in Germany" rule. Dataset locations are fixed once the dataset is created, which means moving requires creating a new dataset in the right region and copying the data. Queries run in the location of the data they reference.
## Keeping it that way
An organization policy with the resource locations constraint can block the creation of resources outside allowed locations, so new datasets cannot drift out of Germany.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A regional dataset in Germany matches the rule; since the location of an existing dataset cannot be changed, the team copies the data to a new dataset and uses a location policy to prevent future mistakes.
- ✗ **B. CMEK for location:** a customer-managed key controls who can decrypt data, not where it is stored. The data remains in the EU multi-region.
- ✗ **C. Reservation location:** capacity commitments and reservations are tied to a location for compute and pricing; they do not move stored tables.
- ✗ **D. Change location in place:** dataset locations are set at creation and cannot be changed afterward, so the data must be copied to a new dataset.

## Key idea
Match residency rules with the exact location (a region, not a multi-region), remember dataset locations are immutable, and enforce with a location policy.
Q009116:
## Controlling and seeing Google personnel access
Google personnel access to customer content is a separate topic from customer access. Customer principals are controlled by IAM and recorded in Cloud Audit Logs.
- **Access Approval** requires an authorized administrator in your organization to approve a request before a Google administrator receives access. Approved requests are logged with Access Transparency logs linked to the approval.
- **Access Transparency** lets you view activity logs of Google authorized personnel: actions related to fulfilling a support request and actions related to service availability.
- Assured Workloads control packages can add personnel access assurances (for example support staff located in a region); Access Approval request conditions are secondary to those assurances.
This is an architecture pattern, not legal advice; the compliance team decides whether it meets a given regulation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. IAM deny policy:** Google employees handling support are not principals in the customer's allow policies, so IAM policies cannot gate their access; Access Approval does.
- ✗ **B. VPC Service Controls:** a perimeter limits API access to services from outside it; it is not a control for approving Google personnel access to content.
- ✓ **C. Access Approval (correct):** the customer's administrator approves each request before Google personnel get access, which is the approval gate.
- ✗ **D. Data Access audit logs:** they record API activity by principals using the customer's resources; the actions of Google personnel are provided by Access Transparency logs.
- ✓ **E. Access Transparency (correct):** gives the customer logs of what Google authorized personnel did, which is the later review.

## Key idea
Approve Google staff access with Access Approval; review what they did with Access Transparency logs.
Q009117:
## De-identification for sharing
De-identification removes identifying information from data. The Cloud Healthcare API detects sensitive data such as PHI in DICOM instances and FHIR resources and applies a transformation (mask, delete, or otherwise obscure). Typical uses are sharing health information with non-privileged parties and preparing data for machine learning.
The operation writes the result to a destination dataset, so the source stays unchanged. Sharing the de-identified dataset narrows the data that leaves the secure environment to what the recipient needs.
Whether the result meets a legal standard for de-identification is for the privacy officer to judge; the architect supplies a repeatable, auditable process.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Manual spreadsheet edits:** a manual process is error-prone, not repeatable and cannot reliably find identifiers inside nested resources and free text.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The Healthcare API's de-identification produces a transformed copy in a separate dataset, so researchers get data without direct identifiers and the originals stay unchanged for care and billing.
- ✗ **C. Edit the originals:** this destroys data the hospital needs for treatment and billing, and it is not a sharing control at all.
- ✗ **D. Contractual promise:** handing over identifiable originals relies on trust alone; a mistake or breach exposes PHI, and the recipient should never receive data it does not need.

## Key idea
Share a de-identified copy, produced by a repeatable service such as Cloud Healthcare API de-identification, not the originals.
Q009118:
## Measuring risk after de-identification
Removing direct identifiers does not remove risk: a combination of quasi-identifiers (ZIP code, birth year, sex) can be unique to one person. Sensitive Data Protection re-identification risk analysis quantifies this before data is shared.
- **k-anonymity**: a dataset is k-anonymous if the quasi-identifiers of each person are identical to those of at least k-1 others. A small k means rows that stand out.
- **l-diversity** extends this by measuring the diversity of sensitive values within each group. **k-map** and **delta-presence** model an attacker with outside data.
- You choose which columns are quasi-identifiers: that states what an attacker is likely to use.
Results guide the next step (more bucketing, removing a column) and give auditors evidence. Whether the result is acceptable is a decision for the privacy officer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Date shifting:** it changes a value but carries no guarantee and no measurement; matching on the other columns can still single out a person.
- ✗ **B. Tokenizing everything:** tokens hide values but do not measure risk, and tokenizing all columns would also destroy the analytic use the researchers need.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Risk analysis with k-anonymity over the quasi-identifier columns reports how many rows share each combination, which is the measurement of singling-out risk the privacy officer asked for before release.
- ✗ **D. Inspection for infoTypes:** inspection finds values such as names or card numbers; it does not measure how unique a combination of ordinary columns is.

## Key idea
Measure singling-out risk of a released table with re-identification risk analysis (k-anonymity) on its quasi-identifiers.
Q009119:
## Generalizing and shifting
- **Bucketing** generalizes a value into a range (for example 34 becomes 30-39), so a person is harder to single out by exact age.
- **Date shifting** moves dates by a random number of days; with a context such as a patient ID the shift is consistent, so sequences and durations are preserved even though the absolute dates are hidden.
- Redaction and replacement remove or flatten the values, so the analytic signal is lost. Hashing a date produces a string, not a date, so intervals can no longer be computed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Date shifting (correct):** preserves sequence and duration for each patient while hiding real dates, which the model needs.
- ✗ **B. Same value for all dates:** every visit looks simultaneous, so order and spacing are destroyed.
- ✗ **C. Hashing dates:** a hash is an opaque string; it cannot be subtracted to produce intervals or ordered by time.
- ✗ **D. Redaction of dates:** deletes the dates, so the order and spacing of visits cannot be known at all.
- ✓ **E. Bucketing (correct):** turns exact ages into ranges, reducing re-identification risk while staying useful for analysis.

## Key idea
Generalize attributes with bucketing and keep time structure with consistent date shifting.
Q009120:
## Where log buckets live
Log buckets have a location, and for each project, folder and organization Logging creates `_Required` and `_Default` buckets, stored in the `global` location unless you configure otherwise. The location of a log bucket cannot be changed after it is created.
## Default resource settings
- For organizations and folders you can configure default resource settings for Cloud Logging: the storage location of new `_Required` and `_Default` buckets, an optional CMEK key, and the default sink. Child resources inherit them.
- Existing buckets and queries are not moved. The setting does not apply to user-defined buckets.
- Admin Activity and System Event audit logs always go to `_Required`, which cannot be bypassed by a sink, so the default location is what keeps them in the EU.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Edit existing bucket location:** the location of a log bucket cannot be changed after creation, so existing global buckets are replaced or left, not edited.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Default resource settings with an EU storage location on the organization make every new project create its `_Required` and `_Default` buckets in the EU, so inherited configuration replaces per-project work.
- ✗ **C. CMEK for location:** a key controls who can decrypt entries, not where the bucket is located; the buckets stay global.
- ✗ **D. Sink to user-defined bucket:** a sink copies entries; `_Required` still receives the audit logs it always receives and stays global, so some log data would remain outside the EU.

## Key idea
Keep log data in a region by setting organization or folder default resource settings for Cloud Logging, before projects are created.
Q009121:
## Immutable storage with Bucket Lock
A Cloud Storage retention policy means objects can be deleted or replaced only once they are older than the retention period; it applies retroactively to existing objects. Locking the policy (Bucket Lock) permanently prevents it from being reduced or removed, which provides write-once, read-many behavior. Google documents this as helping with regulatory requirements such as FINRA, SEC and CFTC rules and with some healthcare retention rules.
## Why locking matters
An unlocked policy can be shortened or removed by anyone with the right permission, so it does not prove immutability to an auditor. Locked retention cannot be reversed even by the project owner; the bucket can't be deleted until all objects have met retention (add a project lien against accidental deletion).
Logs reach the bucket through sinks, which can be created at the organization or folder level as aggregated sinks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Editable BigQuery:** giving owners the ability to correct records means records can be altered, which defeats the requirement that nobody can edit them.
- ✗ **B. Reminders to owners:** a reminder is a process, not a control; default buckets are not seven-year locked storage, and owners could change settings.
- ✗ **C. Unlocked policy:** someone with permission can shorten or remove it, so immutability cannot be demonstrated.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A locked retention policy on the destination bucket makes the logs write-once for seven years and cannot be shortened by anyone, which is the property regulators need to see.

## Key idea
For tamper-proof, long retention, route logs to a Cloud Storage bucket with a locked retention policy.
Q009122:
## Supported products by control package
Assured Workloads publishes, for each control package, the products and API services that are supported. The docs say that if a service is not listed for a package, it is unsupported and has not met all the regional, regulatory or sovereign controls required; unsupported products are not recommended without due diligence and waivers from the regulating bodies. They also warn that unauthorized products may share an API endpoint with authorized products and thus be available to all users.
## What the architect does
- Check the supported products list while selecting services, not after building.
- Enforce the decision: restrict which service APIs the folder may use with the Restrict Resource Service Usage organization policy.
- Use the compliance owner's waiver process if the business needs the service.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Move to another project:** a project outside the folder does not receive the folder's controls, and using it with regulated data would defeat the purpose.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The control package covers only listed services, so an unsupported service must stay away from regulated data, and an organization policy makes the rule enforceable instead of a convention.
- ✗ **C. Shared endpoint:** the docs warn that a shared API endpoint can make an unauthorized product reachable, which is a risk and not an authorization.
- ✗ **D. Automatic coverage:** folder membership does not make a service compliant; only listed products have met the package's controls.

## Key idea
Check the control package's supported-products list and enforce it with service restrictions; unlisted services do not get the package's guarantees.
Q009123:
## Preventive and detective controls
- **Preventive** controls stop a non-compliant action. Organization Policy constraints are enforced at API time: a request to create a resource outside the allowed locations is refused.
- **Detective** controls find what already exists or has drifted. Security Command Center monitors resources for misconfigurations, vulnerabilities and threats and compares them against standards such as NIST, HIPAA, PCI-DSS and CIS; it can define postures and report posture drift, and exports findings to BigQuery and Pub/Sub.
A compliance design uses both: guardrails for what can be defined as a constraint, and monitoring for the rest, with findings feeding a response process. Assured Workloads itself combines the two, enforcing with constraints and monitoring for violations.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Organization policy refuses non-compliant creation (preventive), while Security Command Center surfaces posture drift and compliance findings after the fact (detective), covering what policy cannot express.
- ✗ **B. Both preventive:** monitoring cannot block a change; it reports on state and drift.
- ✗ **C. Both detective:** organization policy constraints are enforced at request time, not just reported.
- ✗ **D. Reversed roles:** the policy is enforced when a request arrives, so it is preventive; Security Command Center reports findings and does not deny API calls.

## Key idea
Org policy prevents; Security Command Center detects. Use both for compliance.
Q009124:
## Designing for erasure
Deletion requests must reach every copy. Two complementary patterns help:
- **Know where data lives**: a stable subject key and a catalog or index of the tables, buckets and datasets holding a person's data, so deletion jobs can target them.
- **Crypto-shredding**: encrypt each person's data with its own key in Cloud KMS; destroying the key renders all encrypted copies, including backups that cannot be edited, unreadable. Cloud KMS key destruction is scheduled, with a delay in which it can be restored, and then permanent.
The design is a technical aid; whether it satisfies the regulation is for the legal team. Per-person keys have a management cost, so teams often apply the pattern to the most sensitive fields.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Keep forever and delay:** an unpartitioned table with a five-year wait ignores timelines for deletion and makes locating records slower, not easier.
- ✗ **B. One shared key:** destroying a shared key would make all profiles unreadable, not one person's, so it cannot serve individual requests.
- ✗ **C. More copies:** every extra copy is another place that must be found and erased, so the burden grows.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Per-person keys let the team make every copy, even immutable backups, unreadable by destroying one key, and an index tells it which stores to clean; together they make erasure practical.

## Key idea
Make erasure practical by indexing where a person's data is and by crypto-shredding with per-person keys.
Q009125:
## Keep data where it must stay and move results
BigQuery runs queries in the location of the datasets that they reference, and a query cannot combine datasets from different locations without copying data. Residency rules are about where personal data is stored and processed, so copies of raw data in another location can break them.
A common pattern is to compute in the data's location and release only aggregated or de-identified results: authorized views, scheduled queries writing summary tables, or Sensitive Data Protection transformations. Analysts anywhere get insights; the raw personal data stays in the EU. Whether aggregates count as personal data is a legal call, so the aggregation level is agreed with privacy counsel.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Copy to a US dataset:** this moves raw personal data out of the EU, which is exactly what residency forbids. Query speed is not the stated priority.
- ✗ **B. Cache in a US project:** caching raw data in US storage is still a US copy of personal data.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Processing in the EU and releasing only aggregates or de-identified results lets the US team do its work while the raw personal data never leaves the EU location.
- ✗ **D. Nightly US export:** the same movement of raw data, automated, so a US copy of everything is created and maintained.

## Key idea
Compute where residency-bound data lives and export only aggregated or de-identified results.
Q009126:
## Tenant-level ownership boundaries
Ownership and sovereignty promises are easiest to keep when each tenant is a separable unit:
- A project (or folder) per tenant isolates IAM, quotas, logs and billing, and lets you export or hand over exactly that tenant's data.
- A key per tenant in Cloud KMS lets you scope access and, at termination, schedule key destruction so any copies, including backups, can no longer be decrypted. That is the evidence of "cannot read it any more".
- Audit logs per project show who accessed the data during the contract.
Row-level separation in shared tables is cheaper but harder to prove and to export cleanly, so it is a trade-off made with the contract terms in mind.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Shared tables and row deletion:** a delete query does not touch backups or derived copies and gives no evidence beyond the query itself.
- ✗ **B. One shared key:** it cannot be destroyed for one tenant without hurting the others, and revoking vendor access is not proof of unreadability.
