- ✓ **A. Flex-start (correct):** it waits for the capacity, so the job can start within the accepted delay, its lifespan of up to seven days covers the runs, it is not preemptible and it is discounted on supported series.
- ✗ **B. Repeated on-demand requests:** this has no discount, no capacity assurance, and requires custom retry automation.
- ✗ **C. Spot:** a preemption could happen at any time and, with no checkpointing, would lose days of work.
- ✗ **D. Future reservation with commitment:** it is designed for large, planned, long-running clusters, and paying for reserved capacity that sits idle between occasional runs is not cost-effective.

## Key idea
Interruption-intolerant, wait-tolerant jobs of up to seven days fit Flex-start; Spot needs fault tolerance and reservations need steady planned demand.
Q009175:
## Feeding accelerators
Accelerators are expensive, so the storage tier must keep them busy. Google Cloud Managed Lustre is a fully managed parallel file system for AI and HPC:
- Multi-petabyte capacity and throughput up to 10 TBps, with low latency and high IOPS.
- POSIX compliance, so existing tools and frameworks work unchanged.
- Integration with Compute Engine and GKE for mounting, and fast managed transfers into and out of Cloud Storage.
A typical design keeps durable data in Cloud Storage and stages the working set into Managed Lustre for training. AI Hypercomputer's guidance for removing I/O bottlenecks also names Cloud Storage Rapid, which suits object-based access in one zone.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More GPU nodes:** they would all wait on the same storage path, so the cost rises and utilization falls further.
- ✗ **B. Dual-region with turbo replication:** turbo replication only speeds up cross-region replication of new objects; it does not raise the read throughput to a GPU cluster or provide POSIX paths.
- ✓ **C. Managed Lustre fed from Cloud Storage (correct):** the parallel file system gives shared POSIX access at very high throughput to many nodes, and Cloud Storage remains the durable home for the recordings.
- ✗ **D. Basic Filestore copies:** a basic tier provides far lower aggregate throughput than a parallel file system, and copying the data for every experiment adds delay and operational work.

## Key idea
When many GPU nodes need fast shared POSIX access, stage data from Cloud Storage into Managed Lustre.
Q009176:
## Choosing the Google AI API by input type
- **Video Intelligence API**: prebuilt analysis of stored or streamed video: label, shot-change, object tracking, logo recognition, face and person detection, speech transcription and explicit content detection, with results tied to time segments.
- **Cloud Vision API**: prebuilt image analysis: labels, face and landmark detection, OCR and explicit-content tagging for images.
- **Speech-to-Text**: converts audio to text; **Natural Language API**: analyzes text for entities, sentiment and syntax.
- **Generative models** on Agent Platform can also reason over video, but need prompting and review of output.
When the input is video and the need is a ready-made detector with time information, Video Intelligence is the direct match.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Natural Language API:** it works on text, so it would miss anything visual and only see the spoken words of a transcript.
- ✓ **B. Video Intelligence API with explicit content detection (correct):** it works on video natively, returns where in the video explicit content occurs, and requires no training or prompt design.
- ✗ **C. Speech-to-Text:** it only converts speech to text and detects nothing in the visual content.
- ✗ **D. Vision API on frames:** it analyzes still images, so the team would have to extract and manage frames and rebuild the timeline itself.

## Key idea
For ready-made detection on video, with time stamps, use the Video Intelligence API; Vision is for still images.
Q009177:
## Analyze versus generate
Google's prebuilt analysis APIs (Vision, Video Intelligence, Document AI, Natural Language, Speech-to-Text) take content in and return labels, text or structured data. They do not create new content.
Generative image models on Agent Platform (Imagen and Gemini) can:
- generate new images from text prompts;
- edit or expand an image using a mask area you define;
- upscale existing, generated or edited images.
Because generated images can be wrong or off-brand, a human-in-the-loop review step before publishing, as in this scenario, is the right control.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Document AI:** it extracts structured fields from documents and does not edit or generate images.
- ✗ **B. Vision API labels:** label detection only describes what is in an image and cannot create or edit pictures.
- ✗ **C. Video Intelligence shot detection:** it analyzes video structure and produces no new images.
- ✓ **D. Imagen and Gemini image generation on Agent Platform (correct):** they create and edit images with prompts and masks, and the human review step covers quality risk.

## Key idea
Creating or editing images needs a generative model; Vision and the other prebuilt APIs only analyze content.
Q009178:
## Speech-to-Text request types
Speech-to-Text offers three ways to submit audio:
- **Synchronous recognition:** short audio, results returned in one response.
- **Batch (asynchronous) recognition:** longer or stored audio, results returned when the long-running operation finishes.
- **Streaming recognition:** audio is sent over a bidirectional gRPC stream and **interim results** return while the speaker is still talking, which suits live captions and voice interfaces.
Text-to-Speech goes the other way, text to audio. Video Intelligence has a speech transcription feature, but it analyzes stored video files, so it is not a live path.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Video Intelligence on saved segments:** it processes stored files after the fact, adding delay and no interim results.
- ✗ **B. Batch recognition:** the results arrive only after the processing finishes, so captions would be minutes late.
- ✓ **C. Streaming recognition (correct):** it returns interim results while audio is captured and refines them, which is what live captions need.
- ✗ **D. Text-to-Speech:** it converts text into spoken audio, the reverse direction, and creates no captions.

## Key idea
Live captions need streaming recognition with interim results; stored audio uses batch recognition.
Q009179:
## Gemini Enterprise versus building
Gemini Enterprise is a managed work platform. Its building blocks are:
- **Data sources and data stores:** you connect Google and third-party sources (for example Jira Cloud), and ingested data goes into dedicated data stores.
- **Apps and the assistant:** an app connects to data stores to serve search results, answers, actions and agents; the assistant is grounded in the stores' content and adheres to the defined security, privacy and compliance safeguards.
- **Agents:** employees can create single- and multi-step agents with **Workflow Builder** (no-code/low-code), Google provides agents such as Deep Research, and admins can register custom agents.
Building the same on Agent Platform is possible and flexible, but costs engineering time that this company does not have.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Gemini Enterprise (correct):** the connectors, grounded assistant and no-code Workflow Builder cover the whole need as a managed product, with no platform to build.
- ✗ **B. Model Garden model with custom connectors:** this is the most engineering-heavy option, and it leaves out the agent-building tooling for non-developers.
- ✗ **C. Custom retrieval app:** it delivers the result but needs a team to build and operate vector storage, ingestion, UI and security, against the stated capacity.
- ✗ **D. Notebooks per team:** notebooks are for working with a chosen set of uploaded sources and do not provide an organization-wide assistant connected to live sources.

## Key idea
For a managed, connected, grounded assistant with no-code agents, choose Gemini Enterprise rather than building on Agent Platform.
Q009180:
## Gemini Notebook Enterprise
Gemini Notebook Enterprise (formerly NotebookLM Enterprise, the name still used in the exam guide) is the enterprise version of an AI research and writing tool. Users add data sources such as PDFs, Google Docs, Google Slides and website URLs to build a notebook, and the AI grounds its responses in those documents to query, chat and summarize.
- It runs in a Cloud-compliant environment: uploaded data stays within your Google Cloud project and cannot be shared externally.
- It is a ready-made tool, with usage limits per notebook and user, not a platform you build on.
Use it for focused analysis of a chosen document set. Use Gemini Enterprise for organization-wide assistants and agents connected to many systems.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Model Garden model with custom retrieval:** it demands engineering and operation of a retrieval service, which nobody wants to build.
- ✓ **B. Gemini Notebook Enterprise (correct):** it grounds answers in exactly the chosen documents, keeps the data in the company project and needs no development.
- ✗ **C. Gemini Enterprise connected to everything:** it broadens the grounding to all company sources, but the requirement is answers only from the fixed document set, and it takes admin setup.
- ✗ **D. Vision OCR to BigQuery:** it extracts text but cannot summarize or answer questions in natural language.

## Key idea
Focused, source-grounded summarization over a chosen document set with no build effort is Gemini Notebook Enterprise; organization-wide agents are Gemini Enterprise.
Q009181:
## Model Garden
Model Garden is a library of models and assets from Google and partners, in which you can discover, test, customize and deploy models. It groups:
- **Foundation models:** pretrained multitask models that can be tuned or customized.
- **Fine-tunable models:** models you can fine-tune with a custom notebook or pipeline.
- **Task-specific solutions:** mostly ready-to-use prebuilt models, many customizable with your own data.
Agent Platform handles deployment and serving with a consistent pattern, and third-party models are scanned for authenticity or malware (for models from Hugging Face Hub, by the hub's scanners) before deployment. For open models, you pay for the compute used by the endpoint.
Choose hosted APIs when you want the least operations; choose Model Garden open models when licensing, control or customization demand it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hosted Gemini with long prompts:** this does not meet the explicit requirement for an open-weight model served on the team's own endpoint.
- ✗ **B. Manual download and serving:** it can work, but forgoes managed deployment and serving and the scanning of third-party models, and puts all operational work on the team.
- ✗ **C. Natural Language API:** a prebuilt analysis API for text; it is not a generative open model that can be tuned and hosted as required.
- ✓ **D. Model Garden with fine-tune and deploy to an endpoint (correct):** the model is open-weight, tuned on private data and served on a dedicated endpoint, while the platform provides discovery, scanning and managed serving.

## Key idea
When control, licensing or customization require open-weight models, use Model Garden to fine-tune and deploy them on an Agent Platform endpoint.
Q009182:
## Prebuilt API or custom model
Prebuilt APIs like Cloud Vision are trained on general categories: labels, objects, faces, landmarks, text and explicit content. They work out of the box, but cannot be taught your company's own classes.
- If the categories are common, use the prebuilt API; it is the fastest and cheapest path.
- If the classes are proprietary (such as your own part numbers), you need a model that learns them: a custom model trained or fine-tuned on labeled examples on Agent Platform, or a multimodal generative model guided by prompts and examples, validated against labeled data.
An available ML engineer and labeled photos make the custom path realistic.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lookup table over generic labels:** "metal" and "machine" cannot be mapped to 40 distinct parts, because the information that distinguishes them is not in the output.
- ✗ **B. Video Intelligence object tracking:** it tracks general objects across video frames and does not learn custom classes from still photos.
- ✗ **C. Natural Language API:** it analyzes text, not photos, so it cannot read the images.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A custom image model, or a prompted multimodal model, on Agent Platform: it can learn the 40 proprietary classes from labeled photos, which a general-purpose label detector cannot do.

## Key idea
Use prebuilt vision APIs for common categories and a custom (or prompted multimodal) model for proprietary classes.
Q009183:
## Agent types in Gemini Enterprise
Gemini Enterprise gives admins central oversight of the agents used by an organization, whoever built them:
- **Employee-made agents** built with Workflow Builder (no-code/low-code).
- **Google-made agents** such as the Core Assistant and Deep Research.
- **Custom agents:** ADK agents hosted on Agent Runtime on Agent Platform, agents built with the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, and conversational agents built with Dialogflow can be registered by admins so they appear in the web app.
Registering preserves the investment in existing agents and avoids rebuilding. Model Garden is a model catalog, not an agent directory.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Register Dialogflow agent (correct):** admins can register Dialogflow conversational agents in Gemini Enterprise, which makes the support agent available without rebuilding it.
- ✗ **B. Team-built front ends:** this fragments the experience and defeats the goal of reaching both agents from one app with central governance.
- ✗ **C. Rebuild in Workflow Builder:** registration of existing agents is supported, so rebuilding wastes work, and agents made elsewhere are not excluded from the app.
- ✗ **D. Export prompts to Model Garden:** Model Garden catalogs models, not agents, and Gemini Enterprise does not list agents from it.
- ✓ **E. Register ADK agent (correct):** ADK agents hosted on Agent Runtime can be registered as custom agents, which publishes the supply-chain agent to the same app.

## Key idea
Existing Dialogflow, ADK and A2A agents are registered with Gemini Enterprise, not rebuilt.
Q009184:
## Reserved capacity for large clustered training
For large, long-running clustered GPU jobs, AI Hypercomputer offers **future reservations**:
- **Capacity blocks:** densely allocated capacity reserved for a future date and time, with exclusive access during the period and unlimited lifespan within the reservation. Suited to pre-training foundation models. A resource-based commitment of one year or longer can be attached for discounted rates.
- **Calendar mode:** reserved clustered capacity for up to 90 days.
Other options trade assurance for flexibility: Flex-start is best-effort, lasts at most seven days and suits shorter jobs that can wait; Spot can be preempted; on-demand is best-effort with no capacity assurance. A quota increase only grants permission to ask for resources, not the resources themselves.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. On-demand plus quota:** quota allows the request but does not reserve capacity, so the start date is not assured and no discount applies.
- ✓ **B. A future reservation with a commitment (correct):** it guarantees the dense cluster on the start date, lasts as long as the reservation, is not preemptible and gets committed-use discounts.
- ✗ **C. Spot VMs:** preemptions would repeatedly interrupt a tightly coupled cluster, and capacity is available only on a best-effort basis.
- ✗ **D. Flex-start:** it is best-effort, so the cluster may not start on the fixed date, and runs are limited to seven days, shorter than the six-week run.

## Key idea
Planned, long, tightly coupled GPU training that cannot wait or be preempted belongs on a future reservation with a commitment.
